utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can we start again, please? Before we give the floor back to you, I would like to be sure that the interpretation is going through. Am I being heard by Colonel Krsmanovic? Do you hear me? Does the Defence hear me? Please sit down. You may be seated. I will ask you to stand up again. You may sit down now, please. First, I would like to be sure that everybody is understanding one another. Does the Defence hearing me? Is the Prosecution able to hear me? Does his Deputy hear me? Do you hear me, Registrar? Do the interpreters hear one another? Very good, thank you. That is fine. I also can hear you. Turning to the Registrar, once again could you call the case that we are dealing with today?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is case IT-96-19 Miscellaneous 1. The Prosecutor of this Tribunal against Colonel Aleska Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to recall that in the current state of affairs this Tribunal, Trial Chamber, has been asked to review, after having received an application on behalf of Colonel Krsmanovic, I recall that in a decision which was taken by a Judge of the International Criminal Tribunal, the decision of 12th February 1996, the judge decided that the transfer of Colonel Krsmanovic to the detention unit which is part of the Tribunal. The decision was confirmed by another decision, an order, which ordered the detention temporarily of Colonel Krsmanovic until 3rd April at midnight. Colonel Krsmanovic has filed an application to the International Criminal Tribunal which he will defend here in this Trial Chamber. I would like, first of all, to be sure that we have the people identified correctly. First, the Defence, you are Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are part of the Belgrade Bar. You are the counsel for Colonel Krsmanovic. Turning to the Prosecution, Mr. Goldstone?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: May it please you, Mr. President and members, I am appearing with Mr. Ostberg.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Goldstone. Mrs. Vidovic, you are the representative that has been called by the Tribunal. Would you introduce yourself, please? MADAME VIDOVIC: I represent Bosnia-Herzegovina as amicus curiae.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Amicus curiae. Colonel Krsmanovic, would you rise, please? Introduce yourself, say who you are, and then state what you intend to submit to the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you please your Honour, before beginning, I have several questions, technical questions, that I would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will give you the floor, but if you do not mind, everybody first introduces himself and I would prefer that Colonel Krsmanovic introduce himself, if that is possible. Colonel, would you please introduce yourself and, in accordance with what the Defence is asking for and what the Tribunal has granted, he will then state his technical observations, but first I would like you to introduce yourself to us. COLONEL KRSMANOVIC: Your Honour, I am Aleska Krsmanovic, son of Ilija. My mother was name was Kosa Zoranovic. I am a Colonel of the Army of Republika Srpska, born on 5th September 1943 in the village of Bijela Voda, municipality of Sokolac, 45 kilometres to the east of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated. Mr. Pantelic, the floor is yours. If I have understood what you said, you would like to present technical observations. Let me remind you, please, that after these technical observations, the Colonel, who has submitted a personal letter to the Tribunal, one of the judges of the Tribunal, it is the Colonel who will state what he has to say and, of course, then the floor will be given to you again to develop legal arguments having to do with the fact in support of the declaration, but now only technical statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to know whether the interpreters can interpret into the native language of my client, that is, into Serbian because we are here for civil matters and with various types of actual proof, every word has its significance. For this reason, I would like to know whether the Registrar has organised this pursuant to the application that I submitted several days ago. I would like to be sure that the interpretation is into Serbian which is the language that my client can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The only thing I can tell you, Mr. Pantelic, and then I can turn to the Registrar for more clarifications and we will decide, that this Tribunal is operating with a Serbo-Croat interpretation booth. Is this all right for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I have heard that the interpretation is into Croatian, which is a foreign language for my client.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the Tribunal is paying attention to your request, but this Tribunal has been operating now this way for several months. I would first like to ask the Registrar whether he could clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. At the request of Mr. Pantelic already expressed in other proceedings that are now pending before this Tribunal, and was an issue raised by Mr. Vujin who was one of Mr. Tadic's lawyers - that is the other Trial Chamber - the Registrar's position, after having asked for two expert opinions, says that those are not foreign languages one in respect of the other, they have common roots, but a great deal of similarity. For this reason, and also because the Statute provides, of course, for the accused being able to hear a language that he understands, therefore, we refused (and this was for much more technical reasons, I could even say for administrative reasons) to get into these discussions. If the Tribunal wishes it, I will ask for evaluations and in any case I am surprised that this request is arriving today, since it has worked with interpreters that were supplied by the Tribunal and I have seen no application about this, which would seem to me that the communication up to this point has been satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, up to this point you did hear the Registrar's answer, did you not? What are your comments about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My observation is as follows. I agree completely with what the Deputy Registrar has said. The only thing provided for in the Rules is that the Tribunal must have proper interpretation and translation for my client. Right now, I have noted here that the interpretation is in Croatian, and I do agree with you when you said what you did, that we must have an attitude which conforms to that Statute and the Rules of proceedings. I really do not know. Among your interpreters, is there one who speaks certain which is the native language of my client? This is the question I am asking. If you do, that is fine, and if you do not we will see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to turn to the Prosecution. Mr. Goldstone, up to this point, have you had any difficulties in communicating during your investigations or during the hearings, during any of the work which your officers are doing, which is of much greater volume than that of the judges? When it comes to this point over the last few months that you have been working, working on transcripts, working with translations in Serbo-Croat, have you ever had any difficulties in this area?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: No, your Honour, we have had no difficulty that has been reported to me by any member of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suggest then that we take a recess for several moments for the Tribunal to deliberate on this issue. The court stands adjourned. (Adjourned for a short time) (10.50 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does everybody hear? The Trial Chamber has taken note of the application by the Defence counsel which was presented at the hearing today, after having heard the Deputy Registrar and the Prosecutor at the hearing. Considering that the statements of the Deputy Registrar and the Prosecutor demonstrate that the Tribunal has never encountered any difficulty with the Serbo-Croat language, and considering that as part of the Tadic affair the Registrar has consulted with a linguistic expert in order to determine whether on the basis of Serbo-Croat, mutual comprehension between Serbs and Croats was ensured, considering that these evaluations are available to the Defence at the Register, if it wishes it, considering that the result of these evaluations were largely supportive of the fact that comprehension between the differences between Serb and Croat are so small that no valid reason could justify the refusal of interpretation into the Serbo Croatian language and that, as a result, in accordance with the Statute of the Tribunal, Serbo-Croat is a language which Colonel Krsmanovic does understand. Considering, then, that the hearing will be based on Serbo-Croatian interpretation, for these reasons we reject the application of the Defence counsel. The hearing now resumes, and I will resume what I was saying at the beginning. I ask Colonel Krsmanovic to rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: One more observation. The Tribunal has taken its decision -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, we have concluded that issue. Do you have other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am not satisfied, however. Sir, before you hear my client I would like to clarify things having to do with the position of my client. Since he is a witness he should be at the witness box and not seated where he is in the place reserved for the accused. This is the comment I have to make.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will answer what the Tribunal has already answered. There is a significant distinction to be made between Colonel Krsmanovic's position in regard of his situation as an accused or as a witness. Mr. Pantelic, if you would please turn around you will see that where he is sitting is not where accused members usually are placed. In addition, he is very close to you and, under those conditions, you can defend him under the best conditions. These explanations now have been concluded. I would like to give the floor to Colonel Krsmanovic who will explain his application. Afterwards, Mr. Pantelic, I will give you back the floor, then I will give the floor to the Prosecutor and then I will give the floor to the amicus curiae. Finally, we will suspend the hearing and I will set the date for the decision. Colonel Krsmanovic, you can now rise and explain the application which you submitted first to Judge Sidhwa and which the Trial Chamber will now hear. I now give you the floor, Colonel Krsmanovic. Colonel Krsmanovic: Your Honours, as I already said, my name is Aleska Krsmanovic, son of Ilija, Colonel of the Army of Republika Srpska born on 5th September 1943 in the village of Bijela Voda in the municipality of Sokolac near Sarajevo. You already have my biographical data and you probably know them by now. While I was performing my professional duties as ordered by my superior officers with the purpose of implementing the Dayton Peace Agreement, I was arrested on 30th January this year and kidnapped by Muslim Police and taken to Sarajevo from Ilidza. You know this and I need not dwell on this, but this is an element, this is a fact, which I would like you to note. Criminal proceedings were instituted against me in Sarajevo for the alleged assistance in the performance of alleged war crimes and I was suspected of such acts, of the act that took place in this unfortunate war. I was then transferred to The Hague because the Prosecutor, distinguished Mr. Goldstone, asked that from the Muslim authorities. Today is the 47th day of my detention here in The Hague. Gentlemen, I would like to remind you of these days. Today is 1,455th day of the war which started on 4th April 1992. When I left Sarajevo and went - I took leave of my family and when I said that not a single world war, not a single civil war ever lasted, ever lasted less than four years, and the family will meet in Sarajevo Omira Masica 4A Street. My Darko is missing now and if I could be on his grave, I would not be able to suppress my feelings, but at this moment I will not cry, I will not shed tears at this moment because I want to preserve my dignity and I think I must bear on my destiny with dignity. I would like to ask you, regardless of the situation, please do not misunderstand me. There have been many victims in the Balkans, regardless of whether they were Serbs, Muslim or Croat. I say that we will keep the memory of the victims alive, and this is a digression for which I apologise to the court but I wanted to say this. So, this is the 47th day that I have been here in The Hague in detention. The Prosecutor has asked me whether I wanted to make a statement in connection with his investigations. I said that I did not want to give any statements. Gentlemen, in view of what I said earlier, God has obliged me to be conscious of every act and every statement and I say that I cannot accept to make any statements, whether I know something or do not know something. I see now that in view of the fact that the Prosecutor has no evidence against me in connection with my alleged participation in war crimes, the Prosecutor now is proposing that I should be delivered to Sarajevo. What am I doing in The Hague and what will I do in Sarajevo? Where are the limits of the denigration of the officers of the Serbian Army and, I would say, an honourable officer and the Serbian people? If the Prosecutor wants to return me to Sarajevo, then I would say that this is a shame for me, for him and for everybody and for this whole Tribunal. I do not fear returning to Sarajevo. I am from Sarajevo. I left Sarajevo on 4th, rather, on 27th March, in fact. I left Sarajevo in a very, at a very sad moment but I left to perform my duties. I belong to Sarajevo. I wish to be in Sarajevo and to live in peace with all people regardless of the situation. I do not know how the Peace Agreement is being implemented, but I can tell you that my heart is in Sarajevo because my memories are there, and a long time that I spent of my life in Sarajevo. I am a professional soldier. I have taken an oath promising to serve my people and my country. I am not afraid of death, gentlemen. I am not afraid of torture because I know that I am not guilty of any crimes whatsoever. What I find most difficult to bear is my separation for the 60th day today because I cannot kiss the grave of my son Darko. I cannot touch my press my lips against the grave marble slab, but my heart is warm. Before this Tribunal I would not like to give any evidence or testimony. I cannot do that because I am afraid that I might condemn somebody wrongly, or that I might give a wrong statement which may come from my ignorance or insufficient knowledge, and I might be saying things which would be wrong, because in my heart there is one thing, that in the Serbian language there is one word, "Keep mum when you are so miserable", and when I come to the grave of my son, I close my eyes, I turn my eyes away from the grave and I look back into my past or the past of my, of my past and, let me be quite frank, since my son Darko was born in Ljubljana, through Sarajevo, through Zadar, through Zagreb and Tuzla, I went back to Sarajevo and my son came with me. He was always with me wherever I went. I held his hand. I do not have anything against those policemen who take me by the hand, I forgive them, but I would like to say when I remember everything that happened to me, then I remember the slogan which says, "Keep mum, you miserable wretch, and suffer, you miserable wretch". Let me also say something which I said earlier, I am not afraid of death, I am not afraid of torture because my last wish is I should be buried alongside my son, Darko, in my native Sokolac. In Sarajevo, I left my apartment fully furnished; in Sarajevo I left my car and I left my memories, everything. I am not alone with experienced all this misery. It was experienced by the Serbian, Muslim and Croatian people. When I buried my son I said: "Let us pray to God that my Darko was the last victim. If there is God, let him hear me", regardless of the religion, regardless of the faith or denomination. However, he was not the last to be killed. What happened, happened. I cannot refrain from thanking Mr. Goldstone - Mr. Ralston, sorry, Mr. Ralston, who found me in Sarajevo on 6th February, in Sarajevo this was the eighth day. This was the eighth day and there are good people everywhere, and I came back to people. After the 6th February, I cannot complain. I cannot complain of the treatment in Sarajevo. I cannot but thank my, the personnel, those who guarded me here in The Hague, and I cannot understand what is happening around me and what has been happening for the 1455 days. I can only tell you that on television here, and I hope I am not boring you with my statement, but I am one of the people who is, who actually asked for a lawyer, so I have now a lawyer, but this was my worst problem. Mr. Stuart Schokrona - I will try to be brief - he was very correct, but the language was my most serious problem. I heard, I saw television here. I saw what happened in Dublin - I saw what happened in Scotland, not in Dublin, Dunhill or Dunblane. Anyway, I would like to ask you to think of what I have said and this completes my statement. I must say that I do not wish to appear as a witness before the Tribunal because I am very much conscious of the role and the responsibility of a witness and I cannot be one. That is all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have you finished, Colonel? COLONEL KRSMANOVIC: Yes, your Honour. I have finished. I have said what I want to say. THE PRESIDING JUDGE: You can now be seated once again. I would like to give the floor to Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have already stated in all my previous -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you would like us to understand each other, you must press the button on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As I already stated in all my previous motions concerning this case, that the position of the Defence is as following: the facts are that Colonel Krsmanovic is actually under the investigation conducted by the Bosnian judicial authorities. According to them, he is a suspect who may be responsible for committing war crimes, more precisely, genocide and war crime against civilians. The Prosecutor of the Tribunal requested from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and judicial authorities of Bosnia-Herzegonia a transfer and a temporary detention, actually the fare from the jurisdiction of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal with his request dated 7th February '96. From my point of view, that was de facto a request for deferral, according to the relevant Rules, more precisely Article 10 - Article 9 of the Statute and 9 and 10 of the Rules. Actually, the Prosecutor possess all reliable information and evidence as provided to him by the authorities of Bosnia and judicial, Bosnian judicial authorities and Sarajevo courts, which means the statements, documents and the other facts. After 47 days of investigation here at the Hague before the Tribunal, we have a response of the Prosecutor dated 27th March this year. So, after 47 days the Prosecutor has his position that, according to all this evidence that he has in this particular case, there is not enough legally grounded reasons for indictment of Colonel Krsmanovic. Consequently, in that mentioned Response to my motion, he proposed that Colonel Krsmanovic would be remanded to the authorities, judicial authorities, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At this stage we can consider that the Prosecutor completed his investigation according to the relevant Rules of this Tribunal, and that the new investigation conducted by the Bosnian judicial authorities would now in Sarajevo be impossible(?). My position, as a Defence counsel, is that we can - and we have actually one very important point in this practice and this procedure of this Tribunal, actually it is not a problem and it is not a mission of the Defence counsel, I mean Defence generally, that the request, the formal request, for the referring to the Bosnian judicial authorities was not made; that was an obligation, according to the Statute and to the Rules of Procedure, which has to be done by the Prosecutor. We cannot consider that if that particular request was not made by the Prosecutor that we formally do not have a request for deferral. Therefore, I wish to refer on the case of General Dukic before this court, before this Tribunal, because it can be important point and a source for the further decisions before the Tribunal. I will shortly tell you why. General Dukic and Colonel Krsmanovic were both transferred from Sarajevo to The Hague, according to the request for provisional measures made by the Prosecutor and transferred to the judicial authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I stress in para 7 that, "the Prosecutor considers these persons to be suspects within the meaning of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal in that he possesses reliable information which tends to show that these persons may have committed crimes or ... (indecipherable) jurisdiction and is currently carrying out further investigation to identify their responsibility for such crimes with a view to preparing indictment against them." So, the main point of the presence of Colonel Krsmanovic here in The Hague was that he was considered by the Prosecutor as a suspect, can be possibly responsible for committing such war crimes, and also General Dukic because this request was made in the name of these two persons, these two officers, I mean for these two officers. After that, I mean after the procedure of consideration in this investigation, we have among all other orders of the different judges of this Tribunal, we have an order for extension of the detention of Colonel Aleska Krsmanovic made by Judge Sidhwa. The one point is very important in that order, is that it being understood that if any time before 4th April '96 the detainees no longer required by the Prosecutor for his investigation or a judge or Trial Chamber for the said reason or any other valid reason may order his release. What we have here as the legal facts, we have one procedure of investigation conducted by the Prosecutor here in The Hague for the Tribunal against my client, Colonel Krsmanovic; at the same time we have the other investigation also conducted by the Prosecutor against General Dukic. What we have are the facts and point of view of these two cases? In the case of General Dukic, it was on the point of view of the Prosecutor enough proofs and evidences and facts for indictment, and actually we have an indictment, an indictment against General Dukic. Against Colonel Krsmanovic, we do not have such evidences and such kind of approach of the Prosecutor until this moment and according to the last Response from the Prosecutor to my motion. This is the main thing which should be important for the decision in that case, that we have actually primacy of Tribunal jurisdiction over the national jurisdiction. At the moment when the Prosecutor requested a transfer of these two persons, these two suspects, to The Hague. After that, from that moment, the jurisdiction of the Tribunal is actual - not the national courts, I mean not the national jurisdiction. After the procedure of the investigation, which is one stage in the general process of trial before the court, the Prosecutor in one case found that, according to the relevant evidences and proofs, one of these two suspects has to be indicted; the other one, no. Therefore, I wish to refer to the case of General Dukic and to request immediate and unconditionally release of my client, because we did not have any evidence and proof against him until this moment and, in the light of the primacy of the Tribunal, we have to create precedent cases for the future because we cannot here make a reference to the previous cases. This is all news for all of us. We have only a few cases here before the Tribunal. So my position that the Trial Chamber should be very, very precise in their decision considering this case. I will not make my position concerning the other Rules more precisely non- bis-in-idem, if we can speak about that, that is a question for the further procedures and it is not a matter of discussion before that Trial Chamber. But I wish to stress again that, according to the order signed by the Judge Rustam Sidhwa, in any time before 4th April the detainees no longer required by the Prosecution, he has to be immediately released, because the Prosecutor has quite enough time to complete his investigation, to make a kind of, let us say, specification of the evidence and the facts that he has in this case for indictment of Colonel Krsmanovic, but we have nothing. In that case, I do not see any legal reason for the proposition of the Prosecutor in his response to my motion that the presence of Colonel Krsmanovic in The Hague is no longer necessary and pursuant to Rule 90(B)(C) Colonel Krsmanovic should be remanded to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why? Why? As we have a primacy of the Tribunal over the national jurisdiction, and after the procedure of investigation that was made by the Prosecutor's Office here, shall the Prosecutor in Sarajevo for the same crime acts which are, more precisely, genocide and war crimes against civilians, under these Rules, this procedure is going on in Sarajevo. So the same crime Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 70 to 74. acts, I mean, possibly was committed by my client here and this was a task for the Prosecutor to find if there is enough evidence for that or not and, more precisely, referring to the case of General Dukic, that General Dukic for the same crime acts, genocide and war crimes against civilians, as the initially investigation was in Sarajevo. So my position is we have one stage which is finished now here, that is, investigation. It is not possible in the light of primacy of the Tribunal to transfer a person or, precisely, Colonel Krsmanovic to the judicial authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to start with the same procedure, with the same investigation, for the same crime acts before the higher court in Sarajevo, about which kind of primacy we are speaking, if it will be done and it will be made by the decision of this Trial Chamber. Where is the position of the Tribunal who has to create international criminal law and precedent cases for the future and for the future cases before the Tribunal, for the future cases no matter where? It is not a case of mad cows or something; this is a more serious thing that we have here. We cannot play with people, with persons, and to send them from point A to point B. Your Honours, we have a very important task here, all of us, to focus all these problems, to be very precise in all our further acts because if we would not be like that, the big question mark will be put under the further work of the Tribunal. Because of that, because we are all professionals here, distinguished professors of the faculty of laws, Prosecutors, worldwide, judges with a lot of experience, we have very simple case and very simple question and the answer is very simple. We have a primacy of the Tribunal; we have finished one stage of the procedure; we have evidences; we have facts; we have de facto request for a deferral, and we have to decide that there is not any legal ground at all that Colonel Krsmanovic should be transferred to Sarajevo under the jurisdiction of Bosnian authorities. The only legal and, let us say, the most important decision in this case, I mean, for the further cases and for the, let us say, position of the Tribunal who has to be serious in all these cases is that, according to the order from 29th February and Prosecutor's Response from 27th March, Colonel Krsmanovic should be immediately released from the detention. This is for the moment, I mean, briefly explained the position of the Defence and I take my right to have another explanations during these hearings. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pantelic. I would like to give the floor to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be brief. The order under which Colonel Krsmanovic was brought to the Tribunal was that issued by His Honour Judge Sir Ninian Stephen on 12th February this year. That was an order under section 90 bis of the Rules of Procedures and Evidence of the Tribunal. Rule 90 bis (A) provides, "that any detained person whose personal appearance as a witness has been requested by the Tribunal shall be transferred temporarily to the detention unit of the Tribunal conditional on his return within the period decided by the Tribunal". "Return", clearly, if one has regard to 90 bis (E), means return to the authorities from which the person was ordered to be brought to the Tribunal. That is 90 bis (E) provides, "that on expiration of the period decided by the Tribunal for the temporary transfer", that would be either 3rd April or an earlier date as decided by this Chamber, on expiration of that period, "the detained witness shall be remanded to the authorities of the requested state unless the state within that period has transmitted an order of release of the witness which shall take effect immediately". No order for release has been transmitted to this Tribunal by the Supreme Court in Sarajevo. The only reason that in our answering motion we moved for an order for return was because that is what is provided in Rule 90 bis (E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. For that reason, your Honours, and in our submission, the Tribunal really has no option and there is no alternative before it but to comply with its own Rules and to comply, in particular, with the provisions of Rule 90 bis (E). With regard to Mr. Pantelic's reference to deferral, in our submission, there was no de facto application for deferral or order for deferral, certainly no de jure order for deferral. It was not requested. It was not in the form that a deferral application would be brought. I would also point out that a deferral order can only be granted by a Trial Chamber and not by a single judge of the Tribunal. Certainly, his Honour Sir Ninian Stephen was not asked to make a deferral application. He was asked to do no more (and did no more) than make an order under Rule 90 bis (A). The order made by His Honour Judge Sidhwa, clearly, he could have no had no intention of departing from the provisions of Rule 9O bis (A). There is nothing in his order to suggest to the contrary. We would submit, therefore, your Honours, that the only way forward in this matter would be to grant an order, to make an order, under Rule 90 bis (E) for the remand to the authorities of Bosnia - referred to as the "requested state" - and that the Registrar should be requested to make the necessary arrangements as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Prosecutor. I would like to call the Amicus Curiae, the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina. MADAME VIDOVIC: Your Honour, I will explain the reasons for the detention of Mr. Aleska Krsmanovic and I will explain the reasons why the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina are asking for his return to our judicial authorities. In accordance with the rule of the higher court, K5796, dated 7th February 1996, the detention was put in force against Colonel Aleska Krsmanovic on reasonable suspicion that he performed an act of genocide, Article 141 of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the crime against civilians, Article 142 of the penal code of Yugoslavia, which the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has taken over as its own law. Let me say briefly that Colonel Krsmanovic is being charged with acts, being a commander of logistics of the Sarajevo and Romania corps of the Army of Republika Srpska. He deliberately in an organised and planned fashion contributed to the execution of orders to attack civilian targets in the city of Sarajevo and other inhabited places in the zone of his operation. He participated in the acquisition and organised the supply of weapons to the combating units; also, he supplied them with ammunition, mines, poisonous gases, and modified aircraft bombs and in this way he contributed directly to the destruction of the city of Sarajevo and the killing of innocent civilians. As a result of such attacks against Sarajevo, some 14,000 civilian people were killed, including 1450 children. Also, a large number of educational, medical buildings and facilities and cultural and historical monuments have been destroyed. The investigation is a very complex investigation. It is still underway and from day-to-day we acquire new pieces of evidence showing the involvement of Colonel Krsmanovic. With the decision of the criminal court chamber of the higher court in Sarajevo detention has been made detention has been made until 4th May 1996, and this is an obligatory detention because these are the kinds of acts for which the death penalty is provided for. Let me also add a new fact today, namely, that the higher public Prosecutor in Sarajevo has filed a request for the extension of the investigation against Aleska Krsmanovic on grounds of suspicion that, contrary to the Geneva Convention of the treatment of prisoners of war, he in his native village and in the municipality of Sokolac he took part in the commission of crimes against prisoners of war, which comes under Article 144 of the penal code of Yugoslavia, which Bosnia-Herzegovina has accepted as its own law, using its own position in the army of Republika Srprska and the fact that he was born in the region. So I would like to state that before the higher court in Sarajevo, we now have an investigation going on which covers also the act which was not included in the material that the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, the Prosecutor did not have at his disposal when preparing his documentation. We, therefore, in the name of the judicial authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina have a firm request that when Mr. Aleska Krsmanovic is no longer needed to this Tribunal, that he should be returned to the jurisdiction of the competent court of Bosnia- Herzegovina. Bearing in mind that the suspect is suspected of crimes for which a sentence of over five years of imprisonment is provided for in accordance with Article 197, paragraph 2, of our penal code, the higher court of Bosnia-Herzegovina can actually extend the detention for a further three months starting from 4th May 1996. If the indictment cannot be made before that last date, he will be released. Let me also say something that Mr. Goldstone also said, namely, that our official authorities have not received any official request for deferral; rather, Colonel Krsmanovic was simply transferred to the International Tribunal in accordance with Article 90 bis (A). We, therefore, ask that he should be treated now in accordance with Article 90 bis (E) and that he should be returned to the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Pantelic, yes, I am going to give you the floor. As presiding judge in this Chamber, I would like to recentre the arguments. You have said, Mr. Pantelic, that this is a jurisdiction which should be exemplary. Thanks for giving me that reminder; I did not actually need it. I would like to clarify the argument so that the position of each side is very clear in the present state of things. The state of things has not been chosen by the Tribunal; this is a statement of observation. In conformity with the Rules of Procedure of the Tribunal, let me remind you that Colonel Krsmanovic, on the basis of two decisions of the judge and at the request of the Prosecutor who made the request to Sarajevo, that the Colonel was detained up to this day in the detention unit under the authority of the Tribunal as a witness. Let me remind you that this procedure is quite possible and quite legal in nature. There is no request for deferral. Colonel Krsmanovic does not play the role of a suspect or a witness. That is the present state of things. Firstly, I would like very much to hear from the Prosecutor, if he would be kind enough to answer this question. Colonel Krsmanovic, as a witness, that you would only agree to his request, as I have understood it, simply because it is the right of the witness not to co-operate with your Office?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, with respect, that is absolutely correct, that we had hoped, and we were kept waiting with regard to that hope until the week of 19th March when Colonel Krsmanovic for the first time informed members of my Office that he was not prepared to be a witness, and he confirmed that clearly to us on 26th March, as appears from the second motion filed on behalf of Colonel Krsmanovic, so that is common cause. On that date we felt that, having regard to the Rules, we could no longer regard him as a witness, and it seemed proper to inform him and to inform the Tribunal that the evidence we had received from the authorities in Sarajevo and other sources available to us did not enable us to come to the conclusion that there was a prima facie case justifying the indictment of Colonel Krsmanovic. It follows, therefore, that, as far as we are concerned, there is no basis for continuing to keep him in the detention centre of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would also like to be sure and ask this question of Colonel Krsmanovic, whom I will ask to stand up and to come closer to the microphone: Colonel Krsmanovic, can you please confirm for the Tribunal that you do not wish to testify? I remind you that you are here as a witness, that is you do not wish to testify, that is, you do not wish to co-operate with the Office of the Prosecutor? This is not blackmail, this is not a threat. The Tribunal here is the guardian of its texts and the proceedings have been drafted in such a way that you have been brought to The Hague as a witness and, as the Prosecutor has just recalled, if you do not wish to testify, which is your absolute and uncontestable right and which will be respected by international law, you do not have to testify if you do not want to. On behalf of my colleagues, so that we understand things properly for our decision, that you do confirm that you do not wish to testify or to co-operate with the Office of the Prosecutor? I am now giving you the floor. COLONEL KRSMANOVIC: Your Honour, since I heard what Mrs. Vidovic said, let me answer, I do not want to be a witness because the role of a commander of logistics does not exist and I was not that, and being an assistant, yes, I was an assistant. That is something else. As for what is being said now, that I have done this, that or the other, I cannot - I cannot accept the role of a witness to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That was the only question that I wanted to ask you and about which the Tribunal wanted to be sure. I am now turning to Mrs. Vidovic. Mrs. Vidovic, the text that I am now going to recall is that, "at the expiry of the date which has been set for the transfer after the detained witness shall be remanded to the authorities of the requested state unless the state", that is, Bosnia-Herzegovina, "has transmitted an order of release of the witness which shall take effect immediately". This is what you said, but I would like things to be clear. At the moment there is no request for release from the requesting state; is that correct? MADAME VIDOVIC: No, absolutely none whatsoever. There is no such provision; rather, there is a request that he should be return to the jurisdiction of our judicial authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic also asked that the floor be given to him and that is what I am now doing, but only to speak about the points that have been raised. This brings other questions to mind to the other people who will give them the floor, trying to recentre legally what we have been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do have a question I would like to ask Mrs. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ask the question and give your explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, as a representative of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, have you been informed of the regulations of Article 29 of the Statutes of the Tribunal, Article 29 of the Statutes?? MADAME VIDOVIC: If necessary to answer this question, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you agreed?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is a bit unusual for there to be a direct exchange, but the Tribunal does want everyone to be able express him or herself, so, Mrs. Vidovic, would you like to answer Mr. Pantelic's question? MADAME VIDOVIC: I have already answered, in fact. I have answered Mr. Pantelic's question. In principle, I am prepared to answer the questions posed by the court, by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal is asking you whether you are prepared to answer Mr. Pantelic's question, but I would like to say to Mr. Pantelic that we are not going to get into a discussion which is over the heads of the Tribunal. I do not want it to be said that you were not allowed to speak or that the Prosecutor was not allowed to speak or that Mrs. Vidovic was not allowed to speak, but I do believe that this is not usual and I will make this as the first and last exception. The Tribunal now authorises you to speak, Mrs. Vidovic. MADAME VIDOVIC: So I have answered, I am fully informed of the provisions of that Article of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My intention has been, and I will remind you of the thesis of my defence, so can we agree that you, as representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina and amicus curiae of the court, you have recognised the primacy of the Tribunal in relation to the specific cases -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I have already stated that there will not be here - please be seated, Mrs. Vidovic, please be seated - Mr. Pantelic, if you wish to ask a question which is an explanation, I am prepared for it to become part of the discussion. You turn to the Tribunal and you will now say what the question is. Thank you. State your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My idea was somewhat different but, all right, I do agree with you absolutely, your Honour. I would like to know what is the position of the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the amicus curiae in respect of the primacy of the Tribunal. Do we agree with that? Are there some questions which have not been clarified?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the position of the amicus curiae is not something that she has to explain; that is for the Tribunal to do. I can tell you this once and for all, and you do know this, there is primacy of the International Tribunal and also concurrent jurisdiction. I recall this point of law to you. What does this mean? It means that national courts can rule on specific cases, crimes against humanity, war crimes, in respect of their national laws. Nonetheless, the Statute of this Tribunal provides for there being at any point in the proceedings that the International Tribunal can bring out its own primacy, but this primacy, Mr. Pantelic and Mrs. Vidovic - I recall this to you - is only executed within a specific framework and this framework has not been chosen by the Prosecutor from the very beginning. It is his choice, it was his responsibility; there has been no request for deferral and, from that point of view, I did want at the very beginning to explain once again what was the legal framework of this situation in which Colonel Krsmanovic finds himself. If the Prosecutor wishes - speaking for him but he can say it himself - to choose other procedural methods, he would have done that. I consider that in the other case that you cited, General Dukic, there was no deferral; the case comes at the initiative of the Tribunal. The Tribunal has nothing to do with this in these proceedings, at least for the time being. We are now working within another context. Colonel Krsmanovic was judged - I will explain it for the first and last time - Colonel Krsmanovic was considered important for the Prosecutor's investigations as a witness. Your client does not wish to testify. This is his absolute right. The Tribunal is here to weigh the rights of one and the others. The Prosecutor felt that it was important for his investigation, that it is his responsibility that he be heard as a witness. I am not going to repeat what the Prosecutor said. Your client, which is his responsibility and his right in addition to that, does not wish to testify to the Office of the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor has, therefore, drawn the relevant conclusions which he has just recalled. Therefore, there is no point in going on. Do you have any other explanations about the other aspects that were raised during this hearing; if so, I am now giving you the floor, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify the position of the defence, I mean very briefly. We cannot -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am asking you to do it briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can I speak here about - PRESIDING JUDGE: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: - about some Articles and some legal institutes? We are here, I wish to stress, for a very, very important moment because we have to decide. It is not a question here, your Honour, that we are speaking about Rule 90 bis (A), (E) etc. We are speaking about the main institutes of the law. We are speaking about de facto deferral that we have here; not de jure. But it is not a problem if one part omits their procedures and duties. I also want to refer to the General Dukic case. Initially we had the same situation as for Colonel Krsmanovic. The authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina provided during all these days all necessary evidences, including for the new investigations and new proofs concerning the crime acts according to the Statute of this Tribunal. After 47 days of investigation this, I mean the part of this Tribunal, the Prosecution Office, made its decision that there is not any legal proofs to do that. But it is a miracle. In Sarajevo, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they have proofs and, according to the primacy of the Tribunal, now we have a position of the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina that they have new proofs, new evidences, they have a new investigation in Sarajevo. At this Tribunal, what does he do? He is silent on that. Forty-seven days, higher, very well-skilled professionals and distinguished colleagues here at the Tribunal made their own investigations, and now we have Sarajevo Prosecutor and Sarajevo court with the new evidences, with the new facts and they wish to put my client under the Tribunal procedure. What is the position and what is the role of the Tribunal? I ask that question. What is the role of the Tribunal? Is the main role and main task of the Tribunal to create precedent cases, or the role of the Tribunal is just to clarify some Rules, 90 bis or 90 (A) or whatever? We have to have an approach, a professional approach -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic - MR. PANTELIC: A few -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I am the Presiding Judge here. I will put myself to remind you that this Tribunal is not standing accused before a Prosecutor whose name is Mr. Pantelic. This Tribunal is responsible for the Rules of law. It is listening to you. I am merely asking you to explain what your thesis is with the proper moderation for a member of the Prosecution's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, but this is the third time that you are excusing yourself. Start your explanations again, please. I do understand that this is important, but it is important for everybody. Therefore, I am asking you to go on. This is the last time that we are going to do this. Conclude what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What I wish to stress is that it is not allowed according to the relevant law institute and the practice of international criminal law to have a decision that, in this particular case, my client should be remanded to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will tell you why, because I refer to the same and very similar case. This is the case of General Dukic and in that light you can consider that this is my oral motion concerning this case, concerning the decision of the Tribunal in that case relating to the case of Colonel Krsmanovic, because basically it was the same position of the Prosecutor, I mean, for, let us say, the possible responsible persons who committed the war crimes. After that we have one who is not and the other who is possible, I mean indicted. So I wish to stress my position on that. Thank you, your Honour. THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Pantelic, thank you. I now turn to the Prosecutor and give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLDSTONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the position should be made very specific and clear, because there has been a certain amount of confusion apparent in some of the submissions made by Mr. Pantelic. The position is that we are not saying that there is no evidence of any kind against Colonel Krsmanovic. We have in the period he has been here obviously sought information from sources available to us, and there is no reason not to say so, including the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. Having given that evidence the best and most earnest attention that we are able, we came to the conclusion that that evidence does not entitle an indictment to be presented against Colonel Krsmanovic. We came to a different conclusion, it is correct, in respect of General Dukic. I think perhaps this is a good illustration of the importance of not attributing in an International Tribunal collective guilt. Our duty given to us solemnly by the Security Council is to individualize guilt. It is a demonstration too that membership of the Bosnian-Serb Army or any other army on its own is not sufficient to attribute guilt for war crimes. The position of this Tribunal under its present Rules is that suspects may not be held pending investigations. I do not want to presume to speak on behalf of Mrs. Vidovic, but as I understood her submission to your Honours, she was not saying that Colonel Krsmanovic is inevitably going to be indicted by the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. She stated that in terms of their law they wish to continue the detention of Colonel Krsmanovic, because they wish to conduct further investigations and further investigations, she said, are presently under way. Whatever the position under the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a matter which she can inform your Honours about should it become relevant. Our position is very clear and I am grateful and thank your Honour for the opportunity of being able to state it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If there are no other comments, I think all of the parties have expressed, we will now adjourn the hearing. The decision will be rendered at 1 o'clock. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: separate transcript on next page) DECISION OF THE TRIAL CHAMBER 2 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Reading of the Decision, the Trial Chamber. Having regard to Rules 54 and 90 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence Rules; having heard Colonel Krsmanovic, his counsel, the Prosecutor and the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina as Amicus Curaie at the hearing today; considering that, under the terms of two decisions rendered respectively on 7th and 27th February 1996, the High Court of Sarajevo ordered that Colonel Krsmanovic should be detained until 4th May 1996; considering that in its decision of 12th February 1996 a Judge of the Tribunal ordered the transfer of Colonel Krsmanovic to the detention unit of the Tribunal, so that pursuant to the terms of Rules 54, 56 and 90 bis of the rules his deposition might be recorded in respect of an investigation by the Prosecutor into crimes falling under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal; Considering that in the orders dated 12 and 24th February 1996, a Judge pursuant to Rules 54 and 90 bis of the Rules the Tribunal ordered the temporary detention of Colonel Krsmanovic at the Detention Unit of the Tribunal; Considering that by the order dated 29th February 1996 the detention of Colonel Krsmanovic at the Detention Unit of the Tribunal has been extended until 4th April 1996, so that he may enjoy sufficient time to consult his counsel and so that the Prosecutor may conclude his investigation; Considering that the applications presented on 19th and 27th March 1996 by Mr. Igor Pantelic, counsel for Colonel Krsmanovic, challenged the presence of his client as a witness pursuant to the terms of Rule 90 bis of the Rules; Considering that the during the hearing Colonel Krsmanovic stated that he was not prepared to appear as a witness before the Tribunal in any case submitted to it; Considering that the Prosecutor believes that the evidence currently in his possession as of this time does not permit the conclusion that there exists the presumption of crimes falling under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal; Considering that it should be pointed out that the Prosecutor, Colonel Krsmanovic and his counsel agree that the presence of Colonel Krsmanovic as a witness is no longer justified by the terms of Rule 90 bis of the Rules; 3 Considering that the application reviewed today as claimed by the Defence, does not fall under Rule 9 of the Rules on deferral but under Rule 90 bis on the transfer of a detained witness; Considering that pursuant to sub-paragraphs (A) and (E) of Rule 90 bis of the Rules, any detained person whose personal appearance as a witness has been ordered by the Tribunal shall be transferred temporarily to the Detention Unit of the Tribunal conditional on his return within the period decided by the Tribunal, that on expiration of that period the detainee shall be remanded to the authorities of the requested state; Considering that the conditions which, pursuant to the terms of Rule 90 bis of the Rules, justify the transfer and detention of Colonel Krsmanovic in the Detention Unit of this Tribunal are no longer satisfied, and that pursuant to decisions of the High Court of Sarajevo dated 7th and 27th February it is, therefore, proper to remand Colonel Krsmanovic to the competent authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina; Considering that the Registrar must take all the necessary measures to ensure the transfer of Colonel Krsmanovic to those authorities it is being understood that the shall transfer shall be carried out at latest by 3rd April 1996 at 24 hours. For these reasons, the Trial Chamber states that the applications submitted by the Defence counsel are well-founded in so far as the presence of Colonel Krsmanovic pursuant to Rule 90 bis of the Rules as witness is no longer required, orders that Colonel Krsmanovic be remanded to the competent authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, instructs the Registrar in concert with all the relevant authorities to ensure with all speed and at the latest before 3rd April 1996 at 24 hours the transfer of Colonel Krsmanovic to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, rejects the other requests. Thus ordered this 29th day of March 1996 at the Hague. The court stands adjourned. (The hearing adjourned).

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing adjourned for a short time) (For Decision please see
